newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Montenegro ruling party snubs Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Montenegro ruling party snubs Milosevic.

text.p: Montenegro's ruling party, in a setback for Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's bid for the Yugoslav presidency, on Wednesday put off a decision on whether to back him.
The leadership of the Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS) said in a statement it would make a decision only on June 23, two days before incumbent President Zoran Lilic's term expires.
It also postponed discussing proposals for amending the Yugoslav constitution, essential for Milosevic to make a smooth transfer from Serbian to Yugoslav president.
Milosevic, the strongman of Belgrade politics for the past decade, is barred from standing again for Serbian president.
To invest the largely-symbolic Yugoslav presidency with real power, he needs the support of Montenegro, the junior partner in the rump Yugoslav state.
The DPS leadership, the Main Board, gave no reason for its decision.
Montenegrin reformists, led by Prime Minister Milo Djukanovic, said they might back Milosevic's nomination but would oppose constitutional amendments.
Milosevic's Socialists say the amendments are needed only to enable Milosevic to be elected by a national election, rather than chosen by the Yugoslav parliament.
But the DPS fears the changes could have wider impact, giving Milosevic absolute powers and reducing Montenegro's impact on Belgrade.

Belgrade has piled major pressure on Montenegro to accept Milosevic and the constitutional amendments through hardline Montenegrin President Momir Bulatovic, a rival of Djukanovic, but he failed to win majority support on the Main Board.
Furthermore, several party districts demanded Bulatovic's resignation. The conflict will also be discussed on June 23.

But Montenegrin reformists have also come under pressure to accept amendments from an unexpected quarter -- former Yugoslav prime minister Milan Panic who told reporters in Belgrade he would run against Milosevic in an election.
By opting for popular vote, Milosevic wants to avoid being held hostage to the whims of the Yugoslav parliament.

But a popular vote would also give Panic, a reformist politician and successful U.S. businessman whose popularity prompted Milosevic to sack him in 1992, a sporting chance to run since he has no party base, analysts said.
The DPS Main Board on Wednesday also discussed a reshuffle of Djukanovic's cabinet, long demanded by hardliners.
But the reshuffle proposed by the Board will hardly satisfy the Belgrade loyalists since all new appointees are Djukanovic supporters. It has to be approved by the Montenegrin parliament.
